blocks.name: Marginalia, three hands
blocks.html:
Reading file · annotated copy · do not re-file

What the paper knew, and when it knew it

Retrospective · 12 March 2026

For thirty-one years the Ledger-Chronicle reported that the cause of the 1974 fish kill was never established. That sentence appeared in eleven separate stories, the last of them in 2003.

It was established. It was established on 9 March 1974, in an internal note that this newspaper had in its possession by the following week. The note recommended that the results not be released until the works had been given an opportunity to comment. No such comment was ever printed, and neither were the results.

What we have been able to reconstruct is not a conspiracy so much as a filing decision: the note went into folder 3, folder 3 went into the morgue, and the story went on being written from cuttings.

blocks.name: Tissue over a front page
blocks.html:
The Ledger-Chronicle
Tuesday 12 March 1974 · City edition · Ten cents

Cedar Reservoir Closed After Fish Kill

Four thousand dead along the western shore. Works manager blames the weather; city engineer will not say what the samples were tested for.

The city closed Cedar Reservoir to all use on Monday after crews recovered an estimated four thousand dead fish along the western shore, most of them within a half mile of the Halloway Chemical Works outfall.

Works manager R. Pettibone said the plant had discharged nothing out of the ordinary and attributed the kill to warm weather and low water in the channel.

The city engineer's office confirmed it had taken samples on Sunday evening but declined to say what was being tested for, or when the results would be published.

Residents of the Cedar Flats district said the smell had been noticeable for a fortnight. One, who asked not to be named because her husband works at the plant, said the water had run yellow twice since Christmas.

A spokesman for the province said the reservoir would remain closed until the city was satisfied it was safe, and that no timetable had been set.

Council will meet in special session on Thursday. The works and utilities committee has asked for a written report in time for the meeting.

The reservoir has supplied the district since 1948. It was last tested in full in 1969, according to the engineer's annual report, which does not list the substances tested for.

Anglers have been asked to keep off the western shore. The medical officer of health said there was no cause for alarm and that the closure was a precaution.

Water is being trucked to the Cedar Flats standpipes twice daily. The city said the arrangement would hold for as long as it is needed.

Council Votes to Daylight
the Buried River

After forty years underground, the Wexford will be opened from the rail yards to the harbour, a decision taken at 1.40 a.m. by a single vote.

By Anneke Ruthven
Staff correspondent · Reporting from City Hall

The vote came at twenty minutes to two in the morning, after the public gallery had thinned to a dozen people in raincoats and the clerk had twice been asked to read the amendment back. When it carried, seven to six, nobody cheered. A woman near the door put her hand flat against the wall as though checking it for a pulse.

For four decades the Wexford has run in a concrete culvert beneath Harrow Street, audible through the grates after heavy rain and otherwise forgotten by everyone except the crews who inspect it. Under the plan approved Friday, eleven hundred metres of that culvert will be opened to the sky, beginning at the disused rail yards and ending where the river already surfaces at the harbour wall.

A cost nobody disputes

Engineers put the work at $184 million over six years, a figure neither side contested. What they contested was the sequence: whether the flood channel is widened before the street grid is rebuilt, or after.

“You cannot phase a river,” said Councillor Miriam Osei, who introduced the amendment and who has argued for the project since her first term. “It is going to arrive whether the paperwork is ready or not.”

Opponents on the finance committee said the estimate omits the cost of relocating two substations and a fibre trunk that follows the culvert for its entire length. The city engineer conceded the substations are not in the figure.

Where the water goes

Hydrologists retained by the province modelled a hundred-year storm against the opened channel and found peak levels a metre below the new embankment, provided the two upstream weirs are removed on schedule.

Removal of the weirs requires a federal permit that has been pending since March. Officials in Ottawa said Friday only that the file is “in the ordinary course.”

Residents of the Harrow Street terraces, whose back gardens end at the culvert wall, will be offered a right of first refusal on the widened easement. Eleven of the fourteen households have already written to the clerk in support.

blocks.name: Anatomy of a headline
blocks.html:
The water beneath

Forty Years in a Pipe

The Wexford was buried in 1986 to make room for a road that was never built. The road is still not built.

By Peter Oyelaran · Photographs by Ilse Marchetti

Meridian City — The culvert is four metres across at its mouth and smells of cold stone. Inspection crews descend twice a year, in pairs, tethered, and they have been doing it since the winter the concrete went in.

What they find is always the same: a river, moving at walking pace, in the dark, under a street named for a family that left in 1949. The city pays $2.1 million a year to keep it that way.

blocks.name: Op-ed and pull quote
blocks.html:
Opinion

We buried it because we could not look at it

By Miriam Osei · Councillor, Ward 6

Nobody in 1986 thought they were destroying a river. They thought they were solving a smell. The Wexford took the runoff from three tanneries and a rail yard, and by August you could find it with your eyes shut from two streets away. Burying it was hygiene, and hygiene was the whole municipal religion of that decade.

The tanneries closed in 1994. The rail yard shut in 2003. The smell went with them, and what remained under Harrow Street was simply a river in a box, doing what rivers do, invisibly, at a cost of $2.1 million a year in inspection and grouting.

The argument against opening it has never really been about money. It is about the discomfort of admitting that a previous council, full of serious people acting on the best advice available, was wrong. I have sat in that chamber for nine years. I know exactly how much that costs.

There is a version of this city where the water is a fact you walk past on the way to work. We are eleven hundred metres from it.

They thought they were solving a smell. The smell left in 1994. The river stayed in the box.
Miriam Osei

Ms Osei has represented Ward 6 since 2017 and chairs the standing committee on water. A reply from the finance committee will appear Tuesday.

blocks.name: Obituary, black-ruled
blocks.html:
Hester Lindqvist

1931–2026

Hester Lindqvist, who as city hydrographer from 1968 to 1991 measured the Wexford every week of its final free-flowing decade and then, under protest, signed the survey that authorised its burial, died on Tuesday at her home in Northgate. She was ninety-four.

She kept the field books. All twenty-three of them are in the municipal archive, in her hand, in pencil, with the water temperature noted to a tenth of a degree and, in the margin for 14 September 1986, the single word enough.

She is survived by a daughter, two grandsons, and a river.

A service will be held Saturday at eleven o'clock at St Brannock's, Northgate. In lieu of flowers, the family asks for donations to the river survey fund.

blocks.html:
The Wexford, from Page A1

“You cannot phase a river,” councillor tells finance committee

the easement, and the clerk was instructed to write to each household by registered post within thirty days.

Mr Vance, who chairs finance, said afterward that he would not seek to reopen the vote but wanted the substation figure tabled before the first tender. “I am not against the river,” he said. “I am against finding out in year four.”

The province's hydrology unit will publish its storm modelling in full next month. A summary released Friday shows peak levels in a hundred-year event reaching 3.4 metres at the Harrow Street gauge, against an embankment designed to 4.4 metres.

Work is not expected to begin before the spring of 2028, and the first eleven hundred metres will take at least four seasons. Ms Osei, asked whether she expected to be on council when the water reached daylight, said she expected to be standing on the bank either way.

Founded 1897 · City Edition · Three Star

TuesdayWater & WorksPrice 60c

The city signed before the ink was dry

A twelve-million-dollar water main contract went to a company incorporated three weeks before the bid closed. Nobody at City Hall can say who read the tender.

By M. Halloran
The tender for the Ninth Street water main closed on a Friday afternoon in March. By the following Tuesday the work had been awarded, and the company that won it had existed for nineteen days.

Its registered address is a mailbox above a dry cleaner. Its sole director shares a surname with a former assistant in the procurement office, who left the city's employ in January and has not returned four calls.

The city says the process was competitive. Asked how many bids were received, three departments gave three different numbers, and the only written record anyone could produce was a one-page summary. cont. p.4
